dataset.name: SPRUCE Anaerobic oxidation of methane mitigates net methane production and responds to long-term experimental warming in a northern bog: Supporting data
description: This data set contains measurements of anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM), net methane (CH4) production, carbon dioxide (CO2) production, and gross CH4 production measurements from the SPRUCE experiment (Hanson et al. 2017). CH4 is greenhouse gas with 45 times the sustained global warming potential of CO2 over 100 years, which may have significant implications on global climate change. The process of AOM plays a large role in the extent of CH4 emissions from wetland environments like those at the SPRUCE experiment site. This study conducted two on different dates. In experiment 1, net CH4 and CO2 production were measured with a gas chromatograph through the peat profile at in situ temperatures of the SPRUCE plots four times from May to October, 2016 (2016-05 to 2016-10). Two treatments were examined, a Porewater Treatment that was a 1:1 volumetric peat:porewater slurry and a No Porewater Treatment that was field-moist peat with no porewater added. Additionally, net CH4 production were measured at frequent intervals (from 4 hr to 9 d) in peat from selected SPRUCE plots from soil collected on October 16, 2016 (2016-10-16). Samples were collected from the SPRUCE plots, immediately made anaerobic, and transported to the University of Oregon for rate measurements within several days of collection. In experiment 2, AOM, net CH4 production, CO2 production, and gross CH4 production were measured through the peat profile at in situ field temperatures once from samples collected in July, 2021 (2021-07). The same two porewater treatments were examined. AOM was measured with a 13CH4 tracer method using a Picarro G2201-i analyzer for isotopic CO2/CH4 quantification with a small stable isotope module attached. This data set contains three data files in comma separate (*.csv) format. This data set is associated with the following publication: Barney, M, AM Hopple, LL Gregory, JK Keller, and SD Bridgham. 2024. Anaerobic oxidation of methane mitigates net methane production and responds to long-term experimental warming in a northern bog. Soil Biology and Biochemistry, 190, 109316. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2024.109316.

measurementTechnique: Observations occurred at The Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) project (Hanson et al., 2017) at S1 bog at the U.S. Forest Service’s Marcell Experimental Forest, in Minnesota, USA (47°30.476’ N; 93°27.162’ W). SPRUCE is an ecosystem-scale study that warms the vegetation and peatland soil profile to a depth of 2 m within 12.8-m diameter open-top enclosures. The peat was heated first at – 2 m for a period of 1 year starting in summer 2014 (deep peat heating phase), then heating of the overlying air began in August 2015 starting the whole ecosystem warming phase of the experiment.

Experiment 1: Net CH4 production in anaerobic incubations with and without added porewater
Methane and CO2 production potentials were measured in each SPRUCE chamber at multiple depths four times through the growing season (May-October) in 2016 at in situ soil temperatures two years after soil warming was initiated. Two porewater treatments were compared, a Porewater Treatment that was a 1:1 volumetric peat:porewater slurry and a No Porewater Treatment that was field-moist peat with no porewater added.
During each sampling event, soil cores were collected from 20-30, 40-50, 50-75, 100-125, and 175-200 cm depth increments (subsequently, depths are referred to by the deepest depth in each increment). All depths were measured relative to the surface of the hollows. The warming treatments increased the depth to the water table during prolonged periods with minimal rain, and only samples collected below the water-table level at the time of sampling are reported here. A serrated knife was used to collect a 10 cm diameter core from the hollow surface to ~30 cm within the peat profile. A 5 cm diameter Russian corer subsequently was used to extract the remaining samples up to 2 m deep. Upon collection, samples were placed in 120 mL serum bottles capped with a 150 mm thick blue-butyl rubber stopper and N2 flushed for 5 minutes within 5 minutes of collection to minimize exposure to aerobic conditions. Additionally, porewater samples were anaerobically collected from 1.25 cm-diameter PVC piezometers at corresponding depth increments (25, 50, 75, 100, 150, and 200 cm below the hollow surface) using a peristaltic pump. Both soil cores and porewater were stored on ice and shipped overnight to the University of Oregon (UO). Extra peat samples were collected from each depth and placed in watertight plastic bags for moisture determination. Water-table and soil temperature data were collected from the SPRUCE monitoring network.
At UO, soil samples were stored within 1 degree C of in situ temperatures (averaged over the prior week for each depth) within 24 hours of field collection and anaerobic incubations commenced the following day. For the Porewater treatment, samples were slurried with a 1:1 mixture of peat and porewater collected from the same plot and depth in a glove box filled with N2 atmosphere with < 5% H2 in the presence of a palladium catalyst to maintain anaerobic conditions (Coy Laboratory Products, Grass Lake, MI, USA). For the No Porewater treatment, peat samples were incubated without additional porewater, which approximated field moisture conditions (≥85% water content in all cases), except in the 30 cm increment where the very low bulk density peat made drainage of porewater difficult to avoid.
Sample bottles were then flushed with N2 for 15 minutes to begin the incubation. Headspace samples were analyzed over the course of 8 days (days 2, 4, 6, and 8) for CH4 and CO2 simultaneously using an SRI gas chromatograph equipped with a methanizer and flame ionization detector (Torrance, CA, USA) with appropriate standards. Total CH4 and CO2 were calculated using Henry’s Law, adjusting for solubility, temperature, and pH. Methane and CO2 production rates were calculated using the linear accumulation (r2 ≥ 0.83 in all cases) of gases through time. Using the extra peat collected in the field, 20 g of each sample was placed in a drying oven for several days at 60 degrees C to determine moisture content.
A high frequency sampling event was also completed on a subset of samples in October 2016 to capture early (<48 hours) CH4 production responses during anaerobic incubations. Peat samples were collected from each plot at random depths (n = 10) and incubated anaerobically without porewater addition within 1 degree C of in situ temperatures. Headspace CH4 concentrations were measured after 4, 6, 12, 18, and 24 hours and 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 9 days. These data are reported in Experiment_1_CH4.csv.
Because net CH4 consumption was consistently observed in samples in the No Porewater treatment, it was verified in bottles with deionized water that added CH4 could be quantitatively recovered over the 8 day sampling period. There was no evidence of gas leakage. Thus, the net consumption of CH4 in this experiment was interpreted as an indirect indication of AOM being greater than gross CH4 production.

Experiment 2: Direct measurement of AOM
In this experiment, net CH4 and CO2 production were measured as above from samples collected from July 2-8, 2021 from the SPRUCE chambers, 7 and 5 years after the initiation of the soil warming and eCO2 treatments, respectively. In contrast to the indirect measurements of AOM described above, in this experiment AOM was also directly measured with a 13C tracer technique. Field sampling was done as in experiment 1, except the 30-50 cm depth was sampled instead of 40-50 cm depth to ensure adequate peat for the incubations. Incubation temperatures were within 1.5 degrees C of those measured in situ over the previous week. The water table was greatly depressed in some of the warmer SPRUCE enclosures, so samples were run from all depth increments, noting if they were taken above or below the water-table level.
Most samples were run without addition of porewater, but the first two samples collected below water-table level (so the corresponding porewater samples could be collected for those depths) were divided into Porewater and No Porewater treatments as in experiment 1. Water tables varied widely by plot reflecting the warming treatments, giving an uneven distribution of sample depths. Most samples were collected from 50 and 75 cm, with limited measurements from deeper depths.
After samples were incubated for 24 hours (T1), headspace samples were measured on the gas chromatograph to determine net CH4 and background 13CO2 production prior to the addition of a 13CH4 isotopic tracer. A 10 mL sample of the remaining headspace was injected into a N2-flushed, 120 serum bottle for later analysis on a Picarro G2201-i analyzer for isotopic CO2/CH4 quantification with a small stable isotope module (SSIM) attached (Santa Clara, CA, USA). Samples were diluted in serum bottles because the analyzer can only accurately assess samples with < 20 ppmv 13CH4.
Before being placed back in the incubator, 13CH4 was added to the bottles to create a 13CH4 headspace concentration of 1000 ppmv. After 48 hours from the tracer addition (T2), the serum bottles were analyzed using the same method except a 1 mL sample from each bottle was stored in a N2-flushed, 120 mL serum bottle to appropriately dilute 13CH4 for injection into the Picarro. To ensure the isotope stock solution was accurate, autoclaved deionized water (DI) was substituted for soil samples following the same procedure as above.
Biogenic methanogenesis heavily favors the production of 12CH4 (~ 99%) as opposed to 13CH4 (~ 1%) (Conrad 2005), but AOM only marginally discriminates against 13CH4. Thus, by injecting samples with 13CH4 and quantifying rates of 13CO2 production, how much 13CH4 was oxidized through AOM was directly measured. The CO2 isotopic discrimination in samples prior to isotope injection (T1) and total CO2 produced from T1 to T2 were used to account for background 13CO2 production.
Net CH4 production was measured by calculating the difference in CH4 concentration between T1 and T2, and gross CH4 production was calculated by summing net CH4 production and AOM. Negative AOM values were set to zero as it was assumed that these values were random variation around our detection limit of approximately 0.012 µmol g-1 day-1. The detection limit was calculated by doubling a one-sided 95% confidence interval of the negative samples.
